what_its_for: This medicine is used to treat serious complications that can happen after receiving the smallpox vaccine (vaccinia vaccine). It helps your immune system fight back when the vaccine causes problems in your skin, eyes, or other parts of your body. It is also used in people who cannot handle the smallpox vaccine well, such as those with weak immune systems or certain skin conditions like eczema. This medicine is NOT used to treat smallpox itself.
how_to_take: This medicine is given directly into your vein (intravenous or IV infusion) by a doctor or nurse in a hospital or clinic setting. You will not give yourself this medicine at home. The nurse will insert a small needle into your vein and the medicine will slowly drip in over several hours. You will be watched closely during and after the infusion to make sure you do not have a serious reaction.
dosing: Your doctor will decide exactly how much medicine you need based on your body weight and how serious your condition is. A typical starting dose is 6,000 units per kilogram (units/kg) of body weight, but your doctor may give you more if needed. The infusion will be given slowly over several hours. Your doctor may repeat the dose if your condition does not improve. Always follow your doctor's instructions exactly.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given in a hospital or clinic by a healthcare professional, it is very unlikely you will miss a dose. If you are unable to make your scheduled appointment, call your doctor or healthcare team right away to reschedule as soon as possible. Do not skip or delay treatment without talking to your doctor first, as this medicine is used for serious medical situations.
storage: You will not need to store this medicine at home. It is stored and handled by healthcare professionals in the hospital or clinic. For reference, this medicine must be kept refrigerated between 36°F and 46°F (2°C and 8°C). It should never be frozen. It should be kept away from direct light. Once the vial is opened, it must be used right away.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor about all medicines, vitamins, and supplements you are taking before receiving this medicine. You should avoid receiving live vaccines (such as MMR, chickenpox, or nasal flu vaccine) for at least 6 months after getting this medicine, as it may make those vaccines less effective. Ask your doctor when it is safe to get vaccines again. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery right away after your infusion if you feel dizzy or lightheaded.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience any of the following during or after your infusion: sudden drop in blood pressure or feeling faint, trouble breathing or shortness of breath, severe allergic reaction (swelling of the face, lips, or throat, hives, or rash), chest tightness or chest pain, severe headache or stiff neck, dark or decreased urine output (possible kidney problems), sudden back or side pain, blood clots (pain, swelling, or redness in your leg, or sudden shortness of breath), fever with chills, or any new or worsening symptoms. Also call your doctor if you feel your condition is not improving.
when_it_works: This medicine starts working during the infusion as it immediately begins to provide protective antibodies to your body. However, improvement in your symptoms may take several days. Your healthcare team will monitor your progress closely. The time it takes to feel better will depend on how serious your condition is and how your body responds to the medicine.
special_populations: Older adults (65 years and older): Use with caution as older adults may be at higher risk for serious side effects such as kidney problems or blood clots. Children: This medicine can be used in children, but the dose will be carefully calculated based on the child's weight. Pregnant women: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant. Use this medicine during pregnancy only if your doctor decides the benefit outweighs the risk. Breastfeeding: It is not fully known if this medicine passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. People with IgA deficiency: If you have very low levels of a protein called IgA, you may have a higher risk of a severe allergic reaction. Tell your doctor before receiving this medicine. People with kidney problems: Use with extra caution as this medicine may increase the risk of kidney damage.
